newsitem.title: GERMANY: Many owed by Vulkan to get nothing - receiver.
newsitem.headline: Many owed by Vulkan to get nothing - receiver.

text.p: The receiver in charge of winding down German shipbuilder Bremer Vulkan warned on Tuesday that many creditors could end up empty-handed when liquidation proceedings were finished.
Jobst Wellensiek estimated preferred claims by creditors at around three billion marks ($1.95 billion) and said that "maybe half" of the company's outstanding debts were guaranteed.
He said there were claims totalling 3.91 billion marks against the Bremer Vulkan holding company alone.
Bremer Vulkan entered bankruptcy proceedings in May after creditors failed to reach agreement on scaling back debt and the company had posted a loss of one billion marks in 1995.
At a meeting examining claims against the company, Wellensiek said that it was unclear whether non-preferred or guaranteed creditors would get any money at all.

Wellensiek was speaking one day before the committee investigating the Bremer Vulkan collapse makes its first report. The committee was set up by the Bremen local government and will hear the testimony of three former Vulkan managers.

Bremer Vulkan's creditors include Commerzbank AG, the shipbuilder's main bank which is owed 539 million marks, the Bremen state bank, owed 230 million marks and the Bremen branch of Dresdner Bank AG, owed 197 million marks.
There are also multi-million mark creditor claims against the Vulkan shipyards and the interim holding company Vulkan Shipbuilding.

Wellensiek repeated his stated aim of continuing to operate the main Bremen shipyard, which provides around 1,000 jobs, and said the construction of two container ships could help to buy some time to save the yards.
He said he hoped to secure approval for remaining European Union funding for the building of two shipyard buildings, which he said could help secure the shipyards' future for the time being.
Management consultants McKinsey had been commissioned to provide a report on the survival chances of the Vulkan shipyards in Bremen and Bremerhaven, Wellensiek said.
Wellensiek said 10 companies were interested in buying Vulkan's defence electronics unit STN Atlas, including Dasa, Rheinmetall, British Aerospace, Diehl and Mannesmann.
